entries.claim: Generating a 64-frame contact sequence as 'sample an initial contact map s_0 from the static object condition (geometry plus hand / role flags), then evolve it deterministically with the local object motion' is supported on TACO: there the evolution from the true s_0 lowers the error from 3.48 to 1.82, and the best of ten sampled s_0, picked with the ground truth, reaches the same error (1.86). On ARCTIC and OakInk2 the evolution shows no measurable benefit over holding the true s_0 (2.21 vs 2.14 and 1.26 vs 1.24; paired intervals contain zero) and every sampled-s_0 variant stays above both true-s_0 rows, so the differences between variants there come from the initial map.

caveats: Best-of-K is an oracle: the sample is picked with the ground truth of the whole rollout. It shows that a good initial map is among K samples, not that the generator finds it.
B0 and B1 use the TRUE first contact map; they are diagnostic rows, not generators. 'Static persistence 3.48' is the true s_0 held for 64 frames.
Raw E_C units differ between datasets (contact-mass scales differ): compare within a dataset, never raw values across datasets.

One training seed (0) and one fixed split per dataset. TACO test = the dataset's test_1 (every group, mesh and subject also occurs in training). ARCTIC test = 44 takes, OakInk2 test = 34 recordings, so intervals are wide.
The evolution is deterministic by construction (one vector field, free Euler rollout); this experiment did not compare it with a stochastic evolution.
The object trajectory is a given input, and the local context of the vector field includes object states up to 8 frames ahead.
G is the static condition: per-mesh surface descriptor at the 512 canonical points, mesh radius and extent, and one-hot hand and role flags (so 'geometry-only' includes which hand and which role).
With one sample (K=1) the generator is above the static true-s_0 row on ARCTIC (3.70 vs 2.21) and OakInk2 (4.09 vs 1.26); only on TACO is it below (2.59 vs 3.48).
entries.claim_as_extracted: Generating a 64-frame contact sequence as 'sample an initial contact map s_0 from object geometry, then evolve it deterministically with the object motion' is supported on TACO, where both stages contribute; on ARCTIC and OakInk2 the evolution stage provides little additional information beyond holding the true s_0 and the error is dominated by the choice of s_0.
entries.correction_reason: Direction and dataset scope match the report (Verdict item 1: 'TACO only') and the tables. Two wording problems. (1) 'the error is dominated by the choice of s_0' is not shown for ARCTIC: the true-s_0 rollout error (2.137) is larger than the single-sample cost (+1.563); it does hold on OakInk2 (+2.849 against 1.243). (2) 'both stages contribute' on TACO rests, for the sampler, on the oracle best-of-10; that caveat has to sit in the sentence. 'Little additional information' on ARCTIC hides a wide interval (-0.257 to +0.107): 'no measurable benefit' is the accurate strength. G also includes one-hot hand and role flags (data.py).

entries.correction_reason: Every number is confirmed in paired_differences.csv and aggregate.csv. The oracle caveat is only in the caveat list; without it in the sentence the claim reads as a generator result. 'Statistically indistinguishable' is an interval containing zero, not an equivalence test, and it is an equality of window-averaged errors: the chosen sample is still 1.748 from the true first map at frame 0 (curves.csv).

entries.claim: With the same evolution, the extra error of a generated sequence over the true-s_0 rollout comes from the sampled initial map (+0.77 TACO, +1.56 ARCTIC, +2.85 OakInk2 with one sample). On every dataset a single sample from p(s_0 | G) is about as far from the true first map as the first-contact map of a random real training sequence of the same object and hand (2.35 vs 2.40; 2.40 vs 2.64; 4.12 vs 4.34), and picking the best of ten samples with the ground truth recovers 95 % / 78 % / 55 % of that extra error. This is consistent with a large part of the multimodality being associated with the initial contact / grasp-mode selection.

entries.correction_reason: s0_err values confirmed (aggregate.csv, reference_baselines_summary.csv). 'The cost of generation is concentrated in the initial contact map' is ambiguous and reads as a statement about the whole error; the true-s_0 rollout still has error 1.82 / 2.14 / 1.24. What the tables show is that B2 minus B1 (same vector field, different initial map) is the sampling cost. No paired test compares sampler and reference; the sampler is slightly closer on all three datasets. The link to 'multimodality' is the report's interpretation (Verdict item 3); this experiment has no mode labels and never ran a stochastic evolution, so 'is consistent with' is the right strength. The reference pool is training sequences of the same group and mesh, not takes.

dataset_differences: Benefit of the evolution stage from the true s_0 (paired B1 minus B0, E_C): TACO -1.664 [-1.776, -1.535], better on 85.2 % of sequences, 47.8 % of the static error removed; ARCTIC -0.070 [-0.257, +0.107], better on 52.2 %, 3.2 % removed (interval contains zero); OakInk2 -0.016 [-0.110, +0.059], better on 37.3 %, 1.3 % removed (interval contains zero).

Best of 10 sampled s_0 + evolution versus the true-s_0 rollout (paired B2 minus B1): TACO +0.036 [-0.043, +0.115] (indistinguishable); ARCTIC +0.339 [+0.213, +0.486]; OakInk2 +1.270 [+1.073, +1.481]. Share of the single-sample gap closed by ten samples: 95 % / 78 % / 55 %.

Sampled generation versus simply holding the TRUE first map: on TACO both K=1 (2.592) and best of 10 (1.855) are below B0 (3.483); on ARCTIC both are above B0 (3.700 and 2.476 vs 2.207); on OakInk2 both are far above B0 (4.092 and 2.513 vs 1.259). Sequences whose best-of-10 rollout beats their own static true-s_0 error: 85 % / 38 % / 16 %.
Evolving a single sampled map versus holding that same map: TACO -1.572 [-1.700, -1.439] (helps); ARCTIC +0.245 [+0.068, +0.436] (hurts); OakInk2 -0.115 [-0.187, -0.048] (small help).

Why the regimes differ, as far as the tables show: TACO is an onset / release regime with large change in contact amount (36 % of test sequences leave firm contact in the window, mean true frame-to-frame change 0.317, static mass error 39.2 falling to 11.9 with evolution). OakInk2 is interaction-only with little to evolve (3 % leave contact, true frame change 0.142, static pattern error 0.0112). ARCTIC does change (42 % leave contact, static pattern error 0.0417) but the evolution does not predict it: it lowers the error on the 107 sequences that stay in contact (2.35 to 2.09) and raises it on the 79 that release (2.01 to 2.20). ARCTIC must not be described as 'no temporal change'.

Per-frame profile: TACO static error grows to 4.41 at frame 63 while the true-s_0 rollout plateaus near 2.1; ARCTIC rollout is below the static curve until about frame 48-49 and ends above it (2.90 vs 2.62); OakInk2 rollout coincides with the static curve (1.70 vs 1.71).
Temporal (frame-to-frame) error of the true-s_0 rollout versus a constant map: equal on TACO (0.318 vs 0.317) and OakInk2 (0.143 vs 0.142), worse on ARCTIC (0.194 vs 0.167).

Test sets are of different size and kind: TACO 364 sequences from 186 takes (the dataset's test_1; 97 % are a take's first contact onset); ARCTIC 186 sequences from 44 takes (dataset train / test labels; only 47 % are a take's first onset, the rest are later grasp episodes of the same long recording); OakInk2 201 sequences from 34 recordings (seeded 80/10/10 split by recording; 99 % first onset). ARCTIC and OakInk2 intervals are correspondingly wide.
Raw E_C units are not comparable across datasets (contact-mass scales differ): the fact that OakInk2 B0 = 1.26 is lower than TACO B0 = 3.48 says nothing about which dataset is easier.

Group-level consistency of the evolution gain from the true s_0: better in 6 of 6 TACO test groups (but only 20 % removed on plate target L, the largest group, versus 42-70 % in the other five), in 11 of 22 ARCTIC groups and in 16 of 36 OakInk2 groups.

Sampler with object-motion context (B3 minus B2): K=1 gain is significant on TACO (-0.236) and ARCTIC (-0.364), not on OakInk2 (-0.284 [-0.747, +0.297]); best-of-10 is worse on TACO (+0.098) and OakInk2 (+0.281), borderline on ARCTIC (+0.142 [-0.005, +0.255]).
do_not_claim: 'Sample-then-evolve works on all three datasets' or 'temporal evolution halves the error' as a general statement: the evolution benefit is a TACO result; on ARCTIC and OakInk2 it is not distinguishable from holding the true first map.
'Ten samples match the ground-truth initialisation' as a general statement: it holds on TACO only (+0.036, interval contains zero); ARCTIC +0.339 and OakInk2 +1.270 are significantly above.

'The generator reaches 1.86' or any wording that presents best-of-10 as a deployable result: best-of-K is selected with the ground truth of the whole rollout (oracle). The single-sample numbers are 2.59 (TACO), 3.70 (ARCTIC), 4.09 (OakInk2).

'The multimodality lives entirely in s_0' (the report's own phrase) or 'all the multimodality is in the initial contact': the tables support 'a large part of the multimodality is associated with the initial contact / grasp-mode selection', no more.

'The future is deterministic given s_0', 'deterministic evolution is sufficient / optimal / necessary' or 'universally deterministic': this experiment used only a deterministic vector field and never compared it with a stochastic evolution; on ARCTIC that deterministic evolution does not beat holding s_0.

'Contact does not move over time on ARCTIC / OakInk2': on ARCTIC 42 % of the test sequences leave firm contact within the window and the static pattern error is 0.0417; the null there is a failure to predict the change, not absence of change.
'Static persistence (3.48) is a naive baseline': it holds the TRUE first contact map, which a generator does not have.

'The learned sampler predicts the grasp' or 'is an accurate initial-contact model': a single sample is about as far from the truth as a random real training take, and FURTHER than the mean training map of the mesh on every dataset (2.350 vs 1.865; 2.395 vs 1.951; 4.122 vs 3.346).
'Object motion selects the grasp mode': adding motion context to the sampler helps one sample on TACO / ARCTIC but makes best-of-10 equal or worse on every dataset.

'The evolution models contact dynamics frame by frame': its frame-to-frame error is no better than a constant map on TACO / OakInk2 and worse on ARCTIC; the TACO gain is in the slow contact-amount trend.
'The evolution is always safe to apply': from a single sampled map on ARCTIC it is significantly worse than holding that map (+0.245 [+0.068, +0.436]).
'Generalises to unseen objects': the main TACO test contains only seen groups / meshes / subjects; on the two TACO groups with no training take the evolution is worse than static.
Any cross-dataset comparison or average of raw E_C values, or a pooled 'mean improvement over datasets'.
Any statement of robustness across seeds or splits: one training seed and one fixed split per dataset.
'Grasp intent', 'human intention' or named grasp modes: the experiment has no mode labels; 'mode' means the spread of first-contact maps across takes of the same object and hand.

'The best-of-10 rollout was compared with the same sample held static': at best-of-10 the held-static row uses its own best sample (chosen by held-static error); only the K=1 comparison uses literally the same sample.

attached_by_the_verifier: Oracle selection is by whole-window error, not by closeness to the true first map: on TACO the best-of-10 sample is 1.748 away from the true s_0 at frame 0 and its curve ends below the true-s_0 rollout at frame 63 (1.950 vs 2.111, curves.csv). 'Reaches the ground-truth-initialised error' is an equality of window-averaged errors, not recovery of the true initial contact. This caveat is not attached to the 1.86 vs 1.82 statement.

Reference baselines (the 'random real training take' and 'best of 10 real takes' rows): the pool is training SEQUENCES of the same group (object category, role, hand) and mesh, not takes (on ARCTIC 1005 training sequences come from 231 takes), and ten are drawn with replacement when the pool is smaller: 51 of 364 TACO test sequences (smallest pool 3) and 25 of 201 OakInk2 test sequences (smallest pool 1) have fewer than ten candidates; none on ARCTIC (reference_baselines.py, reference_baselines.csv column n_candidates). Not disclosed by the extractor.

Window start: the extractor's metric text says the 64 frames start 'at the first firm-contact frame'. They start at a contact-episode onset; on ARCTIC only 47 % of the test sequences are a take's first onset (per_example.csv first_onset 0.4731; TACO 0.9725, OakInk2 0.9900). The fact is in the dataset-difference list but the metric definition and the figure axis label were wrong for ARCTIC (label fixed in the module).

Report prose vs table: the report's Verdict gives the TACO paired interval as [-1.78, -1.54]; the table value is -1.5349612764135008 (section 4 prints -1.535). Use the table (1.53 at two decimals, or three decimals throughout).
The TACO static curve does not keep growing: 4.44 at frame 48, peak 4.47 at frame 56, 4.41 at frame 63. The page text for the time figure should say it rises to about 4.4 by frame 48.
ARCTIC sampled curves are not flat: K=1 rises from 2.40 at frame 0 to 3.96 at frame 63, best of 10 from 1.73 to 2.82 (curves.csv). 'The error is there from frame 0' applies to TACO and OakInk2 only.
